response.text:
I can’t quote the “current” California statute for you because I don’t have web or legal-database access in this session and I won’t fabricate or reproduce statutes from memory. I also can’t reliably decide whether your checkout flow is compliant without (a) seeing the actual flow and (b) checking the exact, up‑to‑date statutory text and any recent regulations or case law.

What I can do right now
- Give a short, non‑authoritative checklist of common requirements that California’s Automatic Renewal/negative‑option rules have historically required (useful as a starting point).
- Walk through your checkout flow step‑by‑step and flag likely gaps against that checklist.
- Draft on‑page disclosure language, consent controls, and acknowledgement text that tends to meet those common requirements (but you should verify against the current statute or with counsel).

Important limitation: the checklist and drafting below are general, based on prior formulations of California’s automatic‑renewal/negative‑option rules and not a quote of current law. They are not legal advice.

Common compliance checklist (summary only — verify current statute)
- Clear and conspicuous disclosure before purchase of material terms of the automatic renewal or continuous service (renewal frequency, price, that the subscription will auto‑renew, and how to cancel). The disclosure must not be hidden in dense text or just in terms of service.
- Affirmative consent to recurring charges (e.g., an unchecked checkbox or a distinct consent button). Pre‑checked boxes or silently enrolling customers is generally disfavored.
- Acknowledgement after purchase that repeats the material terms and explains how to cancel (including a simple cancellation mechanism). For online purchases, an electronic acknowledgement (email or on‑screen) is typical.
- A “simple” mechanism to cancel: the method for cancellation must be at least as easy as the method used to subscribe (if subscribed online, cancellation should be available online), and cancellation instructions must be clear and usable.
- Retention of proof of the consumer’s affirmative consent and the acknowledgement provided.
- For free trials or introductory offers, specific disclosures about trial length, when the customer will be charged, and how to cancel before charge. Some regimes require a reminder notice prior to conversion — check the current statute for any timing thresholds or mandatory reminder rules.
- Any required contact information or toll‑free number/online mechanism mandated by statute/regulation.
- Pricing/renewal changes: requirements often exist about notice to consumers before increasing automatic renewal charges.

What I need to analyze your flow
- A description (or screenshot) of each checkout step: what text is shown, placement and exact wording of any subscription/renewal disclosures, whether consent is via button/checkbox and whether it is pre‑checked, what acknowledgement/receipt customers receive, and how customers can cancel.
- Whether you use third‑party checkout pages and what the customer experience is after purchase (email confirmation, account page, etc.).
- The business’ target customers (California residents? multi‑state?) and the date the flow will be or was used (so you can check the statute effective date if you later supply it).

If you want the exact statute and a legal determination
- Allow me to check the current law (I can do that if browsing or a legal‑database tool is available), or
- Paste the exact statutory text or a link to it here and I will quote & analyze that text and then map your flow against it, or
- Consult a California‑licensed attorney for a definitive legal compliance opinion.

Next step options (pick one)
1) Paste your checkout flow (text + screenshots) and I’ll map it to the checklist and flag likely issues.  
2) Paste the statute text you have (or a link) and I’ll quote and analyze it.  
3) Tell me you want me to draft model disclosure/consent/acknowledgement text based on the checklist.

Which would you like to do?
